extracted.intended_audience: taxonomists, naturalists, and students working on freshwater sponge (Spongilla) identification and description; museum curators
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive standards for diagnosing and differentiating freshwater sponge (Spongilla) species based on morphology, spicule and gemmule characters, skeleton structure, measurements, habitat, and reproductive/biological notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: External morphology (sponge form, surface, oscula, canals, colour, smell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape and surface of the sponge (soft, fragile, amorphous; massive with smooth rounded surface; flat, lichenoid; lobose; filmy, branching, cushions, etc.), oscula size/shape and whether raised or not, oscular collars (well developed or not), presence and character of wide horizontal or broad vertical canals, lateral canals, external membrane, colour (white, yellowish, greyish, blackish, green flush) and occasional strong/offensive smell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout descriptions to distinguish species and varieties (e.g. large deep round oscula distinguish S. carteri; flat lichenoid form with star-shaped oscula for S. fragilis). Note seasonal and environmental changes (colour and form may vary with substrate and water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton structure (radiating/transverse fibres, compactness, spongin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement of radiating and transverse fibres (dense vs diffuse; radiating fibres often crossed by finer transverse ones; transverse fibres splayed out or far apart), compactness of skeleton, presence and amount of spongin (very little to moderate), whether skeleton forms a cage around gemmules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for distinguishing species (e.g. fairly compact skeleton with well-developed radiating fibres in S. carteri; very delicate, radiating fibres in S. crateriformis). Note that paucity of skeleton-spicules can result in softer, fragile varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton-spicules (shape, smoothness, curvature, ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters of skeleton-spicules: smooth or ornamented, slender or stout, nearly straight or feebly curved, sharply pointed at both ends or sometimes blunt, sometimes constricted off and expanded to resemble spear-heads; proportions variable between species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary diagnostic character (e.g. S. carteri: smooth, pointed, nearly straight; S. hemephydatia: smooth, slender, sharply pointed). Immature skeleton-spicules can be mistaken for flesh-spicules—exercise care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of true flesh-spicules
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the species has true flesh-spicules or not; repeated notes like 'No true flesh-spicules' appear for several species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence/presence of flesh-spicules is diagnostic; also note that immature skeleton-spicules may resemble flesh-spicules and cause misidentification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule morphology (adherent vs free, grouping, size, granular coat, external membrane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmules may be adherent to support forming a pavement layer or free in groups; spherical or flattened at base; numerous or few; covered by a well-developed granular coat often with polygonal air-spaces and an external chitinous membrane; external surface may be rough or become puckered when preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangement and covering of gemmules (adherent vs free, pavement vs grouped) and coat structure (granular layers, polygonal air-spaces) are diagnostic at species and subgenus level (e.g. adherent gemmules with multiple apertures and rough external surface distinguish certain species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-foramen and foraminal tubule characters (number, position, shape, length, curvature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of foraminal tubules (often at least one, sometimes two: one at top and one at one side), position of foramen (e.g. at base of crater-like depression), shape of tubule (straight and conical; resembling an inverted bottle; delicate; short or long; sometimes curved), and whether tubule projects beyond the cellular coat or is broken off in dried specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form, number, and position of foraminal tubules are frequently emphasized as key distinguishing characters (e.g. single straight delicate tubule in S. hemephydatia; bottle-shaped tubule in S. carteri; foramen at base of crater-like depression in S. crateriformis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicules (shape, ornamentation, spines distribution, orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules may be cylindrical, constricted in the middle, blunt or pointed, straight or slightly curved; ornamented with short sharp straight spines more numerous/longer at ends than middle (or equally distributed), sometimes forming an irregular circle of strong straight or recurved spines at either end resembling a rudimentary rotule; sometimes free in parenchyma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of spination (e.g. spines more numerous at ends; rudimentary rotule vs no distinct disk) and whether gemmule-spicules are arranged upright or horizontally in the granular coat are important for species delimitation (used to distinguish S. crateriformis, S. hemephydatia, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicule arrangement within the gemmule coat (vertical/upright vs horizontal/irregular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spicules in the granular coat may stand upright or nearly so (more nearly vertical than horizontal) or be arranged almost horizontally or irregularly; some species have spicules arranged in a horizontal external layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An upright and regular arrangement of gemmule-spicules is diagnostic for some species (e.g. S. crateriformis and S. hemephydatia), distinguishing them from others in which arrangement is irregular and many spicules lie parallel to the inner coat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foramen position detail (crater-like depression, rampart)
rubrics_metrics.description: The foramen may be situated at the base of a crater-like depression in the granular coat, sometimes raised round it to form a conspicuous rampart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a crater-like depression and surrounding rampart around the foramen is explicitly cited as a distinguishing morphological detail (e.g. S. crateriformis, S. carteri).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurements of spicules and gemmules (numerical ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit metric ranges given for different elements: e.g. 'Length of skeleton-spicules 0.289-0.374 mm; Greatest diameter of skeleton-spicules 0.012-0.016 mm; Length of free microscleres 0.08-0.096 mm; Greatest diameter of free microscleres 0.002 mm; Length of gemmule-spicules 0.1-0.116 mm; Diameter of gemmule-spicule 0.008 mm; gemmule 0.272-0.374 mm.' (other species have their own measurement lists: e.g. S. hemephydatia: length skeleton-spicule 0.313 mm; gemmule diameter 0.313-0.365 mm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise measurements are provided and used as diagnostic quantitative characters; compare measured specimens to these ranges when identifying species or varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic comparisons and distinguishing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statements comparing species: e.g. 'This species is easily distinguished from its allies of the subgenus Euspongilla by its adherent gemmules with their (usually) multiple apertures and rough external surface.'; 'S. carteri differs from S. nitens in comparatively slender, sharp skeleton-spicules and smooth gemmule-spicules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct comparative phrasing indicates which morphological characters are most reliable for separating particular taxa—use these pointed comparisons when deciding identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenus definition (Eunapius) based on gemmule structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgenus Eunapius: 'Spongillæ in which the gemmules are covered with layers of distinct polygonal air-spaces with chitinous walls.' Gemmules usually fastened together in groups or forming a 'pavement layer'; skeleton usually delicate but sometimes stout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgenus-level assignment is linked to gemmule cellular architecture (polygonal air-spaces with chitinous walls) and arrangement of gemmules; use these characters for higher-level classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation and environmental plasticity (varieties vs species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted varieties characterized by particular features (var. mollis = paucity of skeleton-spicules causing softness and fragility; var. cava = oscula open into broad horizontal canals, glassy appearance; var. lobosa = compressed pointed vertical lobes). Author notes possibility that some 'varieties' may be environmental phases or subspecies rather than true species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution that morphological differences may be due to environment (silica deficiency or other water peculiarities), season, or locality; exercise care before elevating varieties to species—consider co-occurrence and environmental context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and geographical distribution as diagnostic/supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitat notes: ponds, lakes, backwaters, slightly brackish water, on roots of shrubs, on weeds, stones, walls of wells; seasonal presence (flourishes in cold weather or year-round). Geographic distribution lists (localities across India, Burma, Ceylon, other continents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitat and distribution are used to support identifications (e.g. particular species common in Calcutta ponds; presence on oceanic islands is noteworthy). Record locality and substrate as part of identification evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biology and reproductive characters (modes and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of reproduction: (1) regeneration from torn pieces forming young sponges in about ten days; (2) gemmule production (seasonal, numerous towards end of cold weather; gemmules germinate in situ or get dispersed); (3) sexual reproduction (occurring about March and November with eggs and embryos in natural cavities). Timing, germination behavior, and germination in situ are described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproductive timing and the occurrence/abundance of gemmules or sexual stages can aid seasonal diagnoses and understanding of lifecycle differences between species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated fauna and ecological interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of animals associated with sponges (e.g. isopod Tachæa spongillicola in efferent canals; protozoon resembling Trichodina spongillæ; Chironomid larvae like Tanypus and Chironomus; planarian worm; prawns and small fish using oscula for egg-laying). Some interactions may be parasitic, commensal, or beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of particular associated animals may be characteristic of certain sponge species or varieties (e.g. Chironomus commoner in vigorous sponges, Tachæa abundant in S. crateriformis). Note these ecological associations when examining specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule coat internal arrangement and external features (granular layer, polygonal spaces, external membrane puckering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmules have a well-developed granular coat in which spicules may be arranged horizontally or upright; externally a delicate chitinous membrane whose preservation may cause puckering due to unequal contraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic observation of the gemmule coat (layering, polygonal air-spaces, spicule orientation, condition of external membrane) provides diagnostic microcharacters; preservation artifacts (puckering) should be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of type specimens and museum holdings for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of TYPE or types being in collections (Indian Museum, British Museum, United States National Museum, co-types in Calcutta) and references to original figures and descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison with type specimens or authoritative museum material (and published figures) is recommended for confirming identifications, especially where variation is wide.
